title: Oslo Accords
wiki_lead:
The Oslo Accords are a pair of interim agreements between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO): the Oslo I Accord, signed in Washington, D.C., in 1993; and the Oslo II Accord, signed in Taba, Egypt, in 1995. They marked the start of the Oslo process, a peace process aimed at achieving a peace treaty based on Resolution 242 and Resolution 338 of the United Nations Security Council. The Oslo process began after secret negotiations in Oslo, Norway, resulting in both the recognition of Israel by the PLO and the recognition by Israel of the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people and as a partner in bilateral negotiations.
Among the notable outcomes of the Oslo Accords was the creation of the Palestinian Authority, which was tasked with the responsibility of conducting limited Palestinian self-governance over parts of the West Bank and the Gaza Strip; and the international acknowledgement of the PLO as Israel's partner in permanent-status negotiations about any remaining issues revolving around the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. Bilateral dialogue stems from questions related to the international border between Israel and a future Palestinian state: negotiations for this subject are centered around Israeli settlements, the status of Jerusalem, Israel's maintenance of control over security following the establishment of Palestinian autonomy, and the Palestinian right of return. The Oslo Accords did not create a definite Palestinian state.
A large portion of the Palestinian population, including various Palestinian militant groups, staunchly opposed the Oslo Accords; Palestinian-American academic Edward Said described them as a "Palestinian Versailles". The peace process was strained by the Cave of the Patriarchs massacre as well as by Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad suicide bombings and attacks. Far-right Israelis also opposed the Oslo Accords, and Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated in 1995 by a right-wing Israeli extremist for signing them.

Background

The Oslo Accords are based on the 1978 Camp David Accords and show therefore considerable similarity with those Accords. The Camp David's "Framework for Peace in the Middle East" envisioned autonomy for the local, and only for the local, (Palestinian) inhabitants of West Bank and Gaza. At the time, there lived some 7,400 settlers in the West Bank (excluding East Jerusalem), and 500 in Gaza, with the number in the West Bank, however, rapidly growing. As Israel regarded the PLO as a terrorist organisation, it refused to talk with the sole representative of the Palestinian people. Instead, Israel preferred to negotiate with Egypt and Jordan, and "elected representatives of the inhabitants of the West Bank and Gaza".

These pacts established a framework for limited Palestinian self-rule in designated areas of the West Bank and Gaza Strip through the creation of the Palestinian Authority (PA), intended as a five-year transitional mechanism pending negotiations on final-status issues including borders, Jerusalem, settlements, and refugees. Negotiated in secrecy in Oslo, Norway, under Norwegian facilitation beginning in early 1993, the accords marked the first direct bilateral talks between Israeli officials and PLO representatives, culminating in mutual recognition: Israel acknowledged the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people, while the PLO recognized Israel's right to exist and committed to renouncing terrorism and amending its charter to eliminate calls for Israel's destruction. The 1993 signing ceremony, presided over by U.S. President Bill Clinton, featured Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat shaking hands alongside Foreign Minister Shimon Peres, symbolizing a breakthrough after decades of conflict. Oslo II further divided the West Bank into Areas A, B, and C, granting the PA varying degrees of civil and security control in the first two while Israel retained overall security responsibility and full control in Area C. The accords' principal achievements included the PA's establishment, which enabled Arafat's return from exile and initial economic stabilization in Palestinian areas, alongside a temporary reduction in violence that fostered cautious optimism for peace. However, they deferred resolution of core disputes, allowing underlying tensions to persist. Controversies arose from mutual non-compliance: the PLO struggled to curb militant groups like Hamas, with suicide bombings escalating after 1994; Palestinian incitement and failure to revise the PLO charter fully undermined trust; Israel continued settlement expansion, contravening the accords' spirit; and corruption within the PA diverted resources from development. Rabin's assassination by an Israeli extremist in 1995, followed by intensified terrorism, eroded momentum, culminating in the Second Intifada in 2000 and the indefinite postponement of final-status talks, rendering the PA a de facto permanent entity without statehood. Analyses attribute the collapse to structural flaws, including insufficient enforcement mechanisms, mismatched expectations, and the empowerment of rejectionist elements on both sides rather than genuine reconciliation. As of 2026, more than three decades after their signing, the Oslo Accords' interim structures persist, with the Palestinian Authority administering civil affairs in parts of the West Bank amid ongoing challenges including political stagnation, economic dependency, and security tensions following the October 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas and the subsequent Gaza conflict. Final-status negotiations remain stalled, while some states have recognized Palestinian statehood independently of the Oslo process.
